name: CHOOSE

args.name: index_num
args.about: which value to give: 1 for the first, 2 for the second…

args.name: value1
args.about: the first value to choose from

args.name: value2
args.about: more values to choose from

about: Picks one value from a list by its position.

example.why: B1 is 3, so the third value is chosen.

name: COLUMN

args.name: reference
args.about: a cell or range (the formula's own cell if left out)

about: Gives the column number of a cell.

example.why: D is the fourth column.

notes: Without a reference it gives the column of the cell it's in.

name: COLUMNS

args.name: array
args.about: a range or list of values

about: Counts how many columns a range has.

example.why: A1:B4 spans columns A and B.

name: ADDRESS

args.name: row_num
args.about: the row number

args.name: column_num
args.about: the column number

args.name: abs_num
args.about: 1 for $A$1 (the default), 2 for A$1, 3 for $A1, 4 for A1

args.name: a1
args.about: TRUE for A1 style (the default), FALSE for R1C1

args.name: sheet_text
args.about: a sheet name to put in front

about: Writes a cell address as text from a row and column number.

example.why: Row 2, column 3 is C2, written with $ signs by default.

notes: Use INDIRECT to turn the text back into a reference.

name: AREAS

args.name: reference
args.about: a reference; several areas go in brackets, like (A1:B2,D1)

about: Counts how many separate areas a reference has.

example.why: A1:B4 is one block of cells.

name: CHOOSECOLS

args.name: array
args.about: the range or list to take columns from

args.name: col_num1
args.about: the number of a column to keep; negative counts from the right

args.name: col_num2
args.about: more columns to keep

about: Keeps only the chosen columns of a range.

example.why: Column 3 (Pay) then column 1 (Name) spill out as a 5-row, 2-column block; its first cell is Pay.

name: CHOOSEROWS

args.name: array
args.about: the range or list to take rows from

args.name: row_num1
args.about: the number of a row to keep; negative counts from the bottom

args.name: row_num2
args.about: more rows to keep

about: Keeps only the chosen rows of a range.

example.why: The first row (headers) and the last row (Dan) spill out as two rows; the first cell is Name.

name: EXPAND

args.name: array
args.about: the range or list to make bigger

args.name: rows
args.about: how many rows the result should have

args.name: columns
args.about: how many columns (as many as now if left out)

args.name: pad_with
args.about: what to fill the new cells with (#N/A if left out)

about: Makes a range bigger, filling the new cells.

example.why: The one row becomes 2 rows by 3 columns: Apple, Pear, - on top and three dashes below.

name: FILTER

args.name: array
args.about: the range to filter

args.name: include
args.about: a TRUE/FALSE test for each row, like B2:B5="Sales"

args.name: if_empty
args.about: what to show when nothing passes

about: Keeps only the rows that pass a test.

example.why: The Sales rows are Ann and Cat, which spill down; the first cell is Ann.

name: HLOOKUP

args.name: lookup_value
args.about: the value to find in the top row

args.name: table_array
args.about: the table, with the values to search along its top row

args.name: row_index_num
args.about: which row of the table to give back, counting from 1

args.name: range_lookup
args.about: FALSE for an exact match; TRUE (the default) for the nearest smaller value in a sorted row

about: Finds a value in the top row of a table and gives the value below it in the row asked for.

example.why: Feb is in the second column of the table; row 2 of that column holds 80.

notes: XLOOKUP is easier and can look either way.

name: HSTACK

args.name: array1
args.about: the first range or list

args.name: array2
args.about: more ranges to put to the right

about: Puts ranges side by side into one.

example.why: The sales column comes first, then the months: a 2 by 2 block starting with 120.

name: HYPERLINK

args.name: link_location
args.about: the web address or place to open

args.name: friendly_name
args.about: the text to show (the address if left out)

about: Shows a link that opens a web page or file.

example.why: The cell shows the friendly name; the address is behind it.

name: INDEX

args.name: array
args.about: the range to take from

args.name: row_num
args.about: the row within the range, counting from 1

args.name: column_num
args.about: the column within the range (1 if left out)

about: Gives the value at a given row and column of a range.

example.why: Row 2 of the range is Pear, column 2 is its price.

notes: With MATCH it can look up in any direction.

name: INDIRECT

args.name: ref_text
args.about: a cell address written as text, like "B2"

args.name: a1
args.about: TRUE for A1 style (the default), FALSE for R1C1

about: Turns text like "B2" into a reference to that cell.

example.why: B1 holds the text B3, so the formula gives what is in B3.

name: LOOKUP

args.name: lookup_value
args.about: the value to find

args.name: lookup_vector
args.about: a sorted row or column to search

args.name: result_vector
args.about: the row or column to take the answer from

about: Finds a value in a sorted list and gives the matching value from another list.

example.why: 72 isn't in the list, so the nearest smaller score, 70, is used.

notes: The search list must be sorted from small to big. XLOOKUP is more flexible.

name: MATCH

args.name: lookup_value
args.about: the value to find

args.name: lookup_array
args.about: the row or column to search

args.name: match_type
args.about: 0 for an exact match; 1 (the default) for the nearest smaller in a list sorted up; -1 for the nearest bigger in a list sorted down

about: Gives the position of a value in a row or column.

example.why: Pear is the second item in A2:A4.

notes: XMATCH has more ways to search.

name: OFFSET

args.name: reference
args.about: the cell to start from

args.name: rows
args.about: how many rows to move down (up if negative)

args.name: cols
args.about: how many columns to move right (left if negative)

args.name: height
args.about: how many rows the result has

args.name: width
args.about: how many columns the result has

about: Gives the cell or range a number of rows and columns away from a starting cell.

example.why: Two rows down and one column right of A1 is B3, Pear's price.

name: ROW

args.name: reference
args.about: a cell or range (the formula's own cell if left out)

about: Gives the row number of a cell.

example.why: C12 is on row 12.

notes: Without a reference it gives the row of the cell it's in.

name: ROWS

args.name: array
args.about: a range or list of values

about: Counts how many rows a range has.

example.why: A1:B4 spans rows 1 to 4.

name: SORT

args.name: array
args.about: the range to sort

args.name: sort_index
args.about: which column to sort by (1 if left out)

args.name: sort_order
args.about: 1 for small to big (the default), -1 for big to small

args.name: by_col
args.about: TRUE to sort columns instead of rows

about: Sorts a range.

example.why: Sorted by price, dearest first: Pear, Apple, Plum, with their prices beside them.

name: SORTBY

args.name: array
args.about: the range to sort

args.name: by_array1
args.about: the range to sort by

args.name: sort_order1
args.about: 1 for small to big (the default), -1 for big to small

args.name: by_array2
args.about: more ranges and orders, for ties

about: Sorts a range by the values in another range.

example.why: The fruit are put in order of price, cheapest first: Plum, Apple, Pear.

name: UNIQUE

args.name: array
args.about: the range to take values from

args.name: by_col
args.about: TRUE to compare columns instead of rows

args.name: exactly_once
args.about: TRUE to keep only values that appear once

about: Lists each different value once.

example.why: The teams are Sales and Stock, each listed once going down; the first is Sales.

name: VLOOKUP

args.name: lookup_value
args.about: the value to find in the first column

args.name: table_array
args.about: the table, with the values to search in its first column

args.name: col_index_num
args.about: which column of the table to give back, counting from 1

args.name: range_lookup
args.about: FALSE for an exact match; TRUE (the default) for the nearest smaller value in a sorted column

about: Finds a value in the first column of a table and gives a value from the same row.

example.why: Pear is in the second row; column 2 of that row is 0.8.

notes: Without FALSE it may match a near value. XLOOKUP is easier and can look either way.

name: VSTACK

args.name: array1
args.about: the first range or list

args.name: array2
args.about: more ranges to put below

about: Puts ranges one below the other into one.

example.why: Mar's row comes first, then Jan's and Feb's: three rows of two columns starting with Mar.

name: WRAPCOLS

args.name: vector
args.about: a single row or column of values

args.name: wrap_count
args.about: how many values go in each column

args.name: pad_with
args.about: what to fill the gaps with (#N/A if left out)

about: Splits one long row or column into several columns.

example.why: The five values fill columns of two: 1,2 then 3,4 then 5,0, so the first cell is 1.

name: WRAPROWS

args.name: vector
args.about: a single row or column of values

args.name: wrap_count
args.about: how many values go in each row

args.name: pad_with
args.about: what to fill the gaps with (#N/A if left out)

about: Splits one long row or column into several rows.

example.why: The five values fill rows of two: 1,2 then 3,4 then 5,0, so the first cell is 1.

name: XLOOKUP

args.name: lookup_value
args.about: the value to find

args.name: lookup_array
args.about: the row or column to search

args.name: return_array
args.about: the row or column to take the answer from

args.name: if_not_found
args.about: what to show when nothing matches (#N/A if left out)

args.name: match_mode
args.about: 0 exact (the default), -1 exact or next smaller, 1 exact or next bigger, 2 wildcards

args.name: search_mode
args.about: 1 first to last (the default), -1 last to first, 2 or -2 a fast search of a sorted list

about: Finds a value in one list and gives the matching value from another.

example.why: Plum is third in the fruit list; the third price is 0.3.

name: XMATCH

args.name: lookup_value
args.about: the value to find

args.name: lookup_array
args.about: the row or column to search

args.name: match_mode
args.about: 0 exact (the default), -1 exact or next smaller, 1 exact or next bigger, 2 wildcards

args.name: search_mode
args.about: 1 first to last (the default), -1 last to first, 2 or -2 a fast search of a sorted list

about: Gives the position of a value in a row or column.

example.why: Plum is the third item in A2:A4.

notes: Unlike MATCH it looks for an exact match unless told otherwise.

name: TRIMRANGE

args.name: range
args.about: the range to trim

args.name: trim_rows
args.about: 0 none, 1 leading blank rows, 2 trailing, 3 both (the default)

args.name: trim_cols
args.about: 0 none, 1 leading blank columns, 2 trailing, 3 both (the default)

about: Drops the empty rows and columns around the edge of a range.

example.why: A1:A10 shrinks to A1:A2, where the values are, which has 2 rows.

name: TAKE

args.name: array
args.about: the range or list to take from

args.name: rows
args.about: how many rows to keep from the top (from the bottom if negative)

args.name: columns
args.about: how many columns to keep from the left (from the right if negative)

about: Keeps the first or last rows or columns of a range.

example.why: The last row, Plum and 0.3, is kept.

name: DROP

args.name: array
args.about: the range or list to drop from

args.name: rows
args.about: how many rows to drop from the top (from the bottom if negative)

args.name: columns
args.about: how many columns to drop from the left (from the right if negative)

about: Leaves out the first or last rows or columns of a range.

example.why: The header row is dropped, leaving the three fruit rows from Apple down.

name: TOCOL

args.name: array
args.about: the range to turn into one column

args.name: ignore
args.about: 0 keep all (the default), 1 skip blanks, 2 skip errors, 3 skip both

args.name: scan_by_column
args.about: TRUE to read down each column first

about: Turns a range into a single column.

example.why: Read row by row: Jan, Feb, 120, 80 spill down one column.

name: TOROW

args.name: array
args.about: the range to turn into one row

args.name: ignore
args.about: 0 keep all (the default), 1 skip blanks, 2 skip errors, 3 skip both

args.name: scan_by_column
args.about: TRUE to read down each column first

about: Turns a range into a single row.

example.why: Read column by column: Jan, Feb, 120, 80 spill along one row.

name: TRANSPOSE

args.name: array
args.about: the range to flip

about: Flips a range so rows become columns.

example.why: The two columns become two rows: Fruit, Apple, Pear, Plum on top and the prices below.

name: MMULT

args.name: array1
args.about: the first matrix

args.name: array2
args.about: the second matrix; it needs as many rows as the first has columns

about: Multiplies two matrices.

example.why: The quantities times the prices, added: 2×4 + 3×5 = 23.

notes: SUMPRODUCT does the same for two lists without flipping one.

name: SEQUENCE

args.name: rows
args.about: how many rows

args.name: columns
args.about: how many columns (1 if left out)

args.name: start
args.about: the first number (1 if left out)

args.name: step
args.about: how much to add each time (1 if left out)

about: Makes a list of numbers that go up in steps.

example.why: 10, 15, 20, 25 spill down four rows; the first is 10.

name: RANDARRAY

args.name: rows
args.about: how many rows (1 if left out)

args.name: columns
args.about: how many columns (1 if left out)

args.name: min
args.about: the smallest number (0 if left out)

args.name: max
args.about: the biggest number (1 if left out)

args.name: whole_number
args.about: TRUE for whole numbers only

about: Makes a block of random numbers.

example.why: Six random whole numbers from 1 to 6 spill into 3 rows by 2 columns; they change every time the sheet works out again.
